claims.text: Increasing manganese content in chromium-containing steels enhances corrosion resistance in molten fluoride salt.
Manganese dissolves preferentially relative to chromium during fluoride-salt exposure.
Manganese has a lower tendency than chromium to form stable fluorides.
Preferential manganese dissolution limits chromium dissolution and maintains a chromium-enriched surface.
The chromium-enriched surface forms a stable protective oxide or hydroxide layer.
The protective chromium-rich layer impedes further corrosive attack.
316H stainless steel contains approximately 18 wt.% chromium.
Temperatures of 700–800 °C are typical operating temperatures for the proposed nuclear or chemical-processing exposure.
Salt moisture can influence corrosion behavior.
Cooling samples under inert conditions preserves their post-exposure surface chemistry.
Manganese fluoride has a lower standard Gibbs free energy of formation than chromium fluoride.
The stated fluoride thermodynamics make manganese more readily dissolved into molten salt than chromium.
The retained chromium forms a compact, self-healing diffusion barrier.
An Mn-enhanced steel with the same chromium content will lose less chromium than a low-Mn 316H baseline.
An Mn-enhanced steel will form a more robust chromium-enriched surface layer than the low-Mn baseline.
An Mn-enhanced steel will exhibit less mass loss than the low-Mn baseline.
316H exhibits greater chromium dissolution than the Mn-containing HEA under the reported salt exposure.
Low-Mn 316H has greater total mass loss and a thinner or less protective oxide scale than an Mn-enhanced formulation.
The proposed mechanism applies to molten fluoride salts and analogous aggressive chemical-processing fluids.
Salt impurities and temperature can alter fluoride-salt corrosion behavior.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes preferential Mn dissolution to a lower tendency to form stable fluorides, whereas the mechanism invokes a lower standard Gibbs free energy for Mn-fluoride formation. A lower formation free energy ordinarily indicates greater fluoride stability, so the two thermodynamic descriptions conflict.
